meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sometimes I sit and think, and sometimes I just sit'?
meta.ogDescription: Not A. A. Milne. An anonymous folk saying from a 1905 Boston Record anecdote about a Maine fisherman, later misattributed to Pooh.

answer.label: Not A. A. Milne — an anonymous folk saying
answer.authorDates: First recorded February 1905 · American newspaper humor
answer.sourceLine: The line is not from A. A. Milne or Winnie-the-Pooh. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest known version appeared in the Boston Record and was reprinted in newspapers in February 1905 — an old Maine fisherman’s reply, “Oh, sometimes I sit and think, and then again I just sit.” It was popularized by a 1906 Punch cartoon and only attached to Milne around 2006. It appears in none of his books.

source.excerpt: A bond salesman, just back from Maine, told of asking an old fisherman what he did with himself evenings. “Oh,” said the fisherman, “sometimes I sit and think, and then again I just sit.”
trail: February 1905: the earliest known version runs in the Boston Record and is reprinted in papers such as the Pittsburg Press, crediting an anonymous old Maine fisherman, per Quote Investigator.
24 October 1906: William Gunning King’s cartoon in Punch carries the caption “sometimes I sits and thinks; and then again I just sits,” which spread the saying widely (Barry Popik).

1915: L. M. Montgomery folds a dialect variant into Anne of the Island — “Part of the time I sits and thinks and the rest I jest sits” — showing it was already common folk currency (Quote Investigator).
c. 2006 onward: the line is retro-fitted onto A. A. Milne and Winnie-the-Pooh (and, separately, onto Satchel Paige), though it appears in none of Milne’s books and is absent from his Wikiquote page.
source.excerptNote: Reconstructed from the 1905 Boston Record anecdote as reprinted in U.S. newspapers; the modern polished form — “sometimes I sit and think, and sometimes I just sit” — is a later smoothing of this joke.

author.name: Anonymous (American folk saying)
author.heading: An orphan folk saying, wrongly adopted
author.metaLine: First recorded 1905 · U.S. newspaper humor, popularized by Punch (1906)
author.bio: This is a piece of turn-of-the-century American folk wit, not a line by any single author. It surfaces first as an old Maine fisherman’s deadpan reply in a 1905 Boston Record anecdote, then spreads through a 1906 Punch cartoon by William Gunning King. Like many orphan sayings, it was later pinned on famous names — A. A. Milne and Satchel Paige among them — who had nothing to do with it.

misattribution.heading: How Pooh got the credit
misattribution.intro: A feel-good one-liner with no owner is exactly the kind of quote that drifts toward famous, gentle names. This one landed on A. A. Milne — but it predates Winnie-the-Pooh by two decades.

items.why: The line appears in none of Milne’s books and is absent from his Wikiquote page; the attribution only emerges around 2006, per Quote Investigator. The saying was already in print in 1905, when Milne was 23 and Pooh was two decades away.
The baseball pitcher gets credit in some collections (around 2009), but the wording long predates him — another famous name attached to an already-old saying, per Quote Investigator.

Punch (1906) and a September 1911 Woodrow Wilson political usage (“a conservative man is a man who just sits and thinks, mostly sits”) helped circulate the line, but they repeat an existing joke rather than coin it, per Quote Investigator; the Boston Record version predates them (Barry Popik).

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is anonymous: an old Maine fisherman’s deadpan reply, first printed in the Boston Record in February 1905, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Pooh
lead: The saying works because it flatters idleness as a kind of wisdom — which is precisely the register of Winnie-the-Pooh, a bear “of very little brain” who is content to do nothing in particular. That tonal match is why the internet finds Milne a plausible home for it, even though the words are a New England fisherman’s joke from 1905.
context.pull: A folk joke about doing nothing, mistaken for the philosophy of a bear who does nothing.
